Reuters reports that Russia's antitrust regulator has formally opened an investigation into Apple for failing to pre-install the state-backed instant messaging app MAX and the Russian app store RuStore on its devices. Below is the detailed content.

Russia Opens Antitrust Probe Against Apple

Since Russia passed a law in 2019 requiring device manufacturers to pre-load local apps on products sold domestically, Apple and Russian authorities have been locked in a protracted tug-of-war.

When the law took effect in 2021, Apple reached an arrangement whereby Russian users setting up a new iPhone would be shown a list of recommended Russian-developed apps during setup, rather than having them automatically pre-installed.

In March 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Apple halted product sales and exports in the country, and removed the RT News and Sputnik News apps from the App Store outside Russia. That September, Apple also removed several apps owned by Russian tech firm VK, citing UK sanctions.

Last year, Russia began requiring all new smartphones and tablets sold in the country to come pre-installed with the state-backed instant messaging app MAX, while also extending the mandate to pre-install the RuStore app store to Apple devices. Apple has not complied with either requirement.

Tensions escalated further in June, when Apple pulled MAX from the Russian App Store, followed later that same month by the removal of several apps developed by VK. Apple said the removals were to comply with sanctions.

This prompted Russia's Federal Antimonopoly Service (FAS) to issue an order requiring the company to address what it described as discriminatory treatment of local software by July 15. Apple reportedly offered partial compliance, allowing a Russian search engine to be pre-installed in iOS 26.6, but did not implement the requirements regarding MAX and RuStore.

Now, according to Reuters, Russia has formally opened an antitrust investigation into Apple over its failure to fully comply with the warning.

It remains unclear what penalties Apple could face if Russia finds it in violation of its competition laws. In 2024, Russia calculated that Google owed approximately 20 decillion dollars (a 2 followed by 33 zeros) in accumulated fines for years of refusing to restore blocked Russian state and pro-Kremlin channels on YouTube.

Apple has not yet responded to the inquiry.
